Houses, machines, clothes, and so on differ from natural “things” only because human beings use them—that is, because the interaction between humanity and the natural world continues.
For a bird, for example, there is essentially no difference today between a telegraph wire on which it perches and the branch of a tree.

And if humanity disappeared, everything it had created—houses, machines, and so on—would in principle become indistinguishable from piles of stone or iron, mountains, shells, and other natural objects.
After all, these things are made from the very same “materials” that existed before human beings appeared.
A ton of steel arranged into rotary printing machinery differs essentially and radically from an ordinary ton of steel only because human beings use it to print newspapers.
Likewise, a house differs from a “natural” cave only because human beings use it as a home.
So what is dialectical first is the interaction with the non-dialectical natural world.
What is dialectical secondarily, or by derivation, is first the inseparable cause of that interaction—the human being—and then its inseparable “effect”—the human world.
We can say that human beings and the human world they create, that is, the historical world, are dialectical only because they are bound up with this interaction.
What is specifically “human” in humanity—the dialectical character of human beings and of the historical world—comes into existence with this interaction and disappears with it.

Conversely, dialectic is nothing other than this interaction taken as a whole: an interaction that includes both the human being who brings it about and the historical world that the human being produces.

For although human beings and the historical world cannot exist apart from interaction with the natural world, that interaction cannot exist apart from human beings and the historical world they create either.
To speak of interaction—that is, of dialectic—is therefore to speak of human beings and the historical world.

It is to speak of human beings insofar as they create the historical world through their interaction with the natural world, and of the historical world insofar as human beings create it through that same interaction.
In other words, to speak about dialectic is to speak about human beings insofar as they differ from animals, plants, and other natural “things.”
And it is to speak about the historical world insofar as it differs from the natural world.
So what exactly is this “historical world”?
First of all, it is the “ideal” world of human “culture”: the world of science, literature, art, religion, sport, and so on—in short, the world of what Marx called “ideological superstructures.”
At bottom, this is the world of human discourse or, more precisely, the world of the meaning carried by that discourse.
Discourse, or logos, exists only through articulated sounds—“words”—or through signs—“letters”—written on some physical surface, or finally through physico-chemical processes in a brain—“thoughts.”
Meaning physically “adds” nothing to any of these things.
Yet meaning is neither a sound, nor a sign, nor a chemical process. It is something entirely other.

And it is only the presence of this “other” that transforms sounds, signs, and chemical processes into meaningful discourse: something that exists only through human beings, in human beings, and for human beings.
Meaningful discourse is the result—or, if you prefer, one of the forms—of the dialectical interaction between human beings and the natural world.
But just as this discourse cannot exist without human beings, human beings could not exist without this discourse, and neither could the historical world they have built.
We can therefore also say that the historical world is first of all the world of human discourse—or, more exactly, the world of its meaning.
Only the meaning of discourse is genuinely human and therefore historical and dialectical.
Meaningful discourse is always dialectical, and dialectic is realized both in meaningful discourse and in the “ideal” world that discourse creates.
But this ideal world is not the only embodiment of dialectic.
The historical world is larger than the “ideal” world.
It rests on a “real” human world, which is no longer the world of discourse but the world of work and struggle.
This real world provides the actual foundation for the “ideological superstructure” of the “ideal” world of discourse and culture in general.
Without this real historical world, the ideal historical world could not exist.
Conversely, this real world is human, historical, and dialectical only because it supports that ideological superstructure.
Human beings speak because they work and struggle.
Yet they work and struggle as human beings, rather than as animals, precisely because they do not merely work and struggle. They also speak about their work and their struggle.
And they can speak about them only because they work and struggle differently from animals.
Here again we encounter the elusive “something” mentioned earlier—the very thing that realizes what we call dialectic.
There is no need to repeat what has already been said.
We need only note that the presence of this “something other” transforms a collection of “human” individuals into genuinely human societies and States—that is, historical or dialectical ones.
It likewise transforms the changes those individuals make to the natural world into genuinely human, and therefore historical or dialectical, technology.
Since the real historical world is based on work, we can call it the technical or “economic” world.
But since it is also based on struggle, we can call it the “political” world—or the “historical” world in the narrower sense.
It is obvious that there is no politics or technology without human beings. But we must add that there are no human beings without technology and politics either.
Like meaningful discourse and “culture” in general, technology and politics are forms of interaction with the natural world.
The “technical” human being—the person who works—and the “political” human being—the person who struggles—are therefore every bit as dialectical as the “cultural” human being—the person who speaks.
And the historical world of technology and politics is just as dialectical as the ideal historical world of meaningful discourse.

Conversely, dialectic is realized not only in human discourse and in the “ideal” world that discourse constructs. It is also realized in the real historical world of politics and technology created through human work and struggle.
Dialectic, then, is nothing other than the human being creating the historical world, both ideal and real.
Or, which comes to the same thing, dialectic is nothing other than the historical world created by human beings—or, more precisely, the historical world that human beings are continually creating.
It is therefore the process through which human beings create the historical world—and create themselves only in and through that process of creating the world.
But even this process does not completely exhaust dialectic.
In a certain sense, the natural world as a whole also realizes dialectic insofar as it includes human beings and therefore enters into interaction with them.
The historical—that is, human and dialectical—world in the broad sense is not only created by human beings.
To turn a natural thing into a “cultural” or “historical,” and therefore dialectical, thing, human beings do not necessarily have to alter it physically.
It is enough for them to enter into a real relation with it, provided that what enters into that relation is genuinely human and not merely the human animal body.
The fact that human beings breathe air does not make air “historical.” Animals breathe it too.

But the rock on which the Acropolis of Athens stands is just as “historical” as the building erected on it. It realizes dialectic just as much—not insofar as it is a natural rock, but insofar as it functions, so to speak, as the “foundation” of the Parthenon.
The sea is, in itself, a purely natural “thing.”
By itself it is not dialectical in any way, and nothing that happens within it, such as the cycle of the tides, has anything to do with dialectic.
Nor does the sea become dialectical merely because people decide to swim in it, since animals swim too.
But human beings do not merely splash around in the sea. They also work on and around it, and they struggle over it.
Since human work and struggle are dialectical, “working at sea” and “fighting over the sea” are dialectical too.
And because the “sea” enters into this dialectical phenomenon, the sea itself thereby becomes dialectical.
But work at sea, although it is specifically work at sea rather than somewhere else, is dialectical not because it takes place at sea, but because it is work at sea.
The same applies to struggle over the sea.
The Mediterranean, for example, was not the same thing for the Greeks of Pericles’ time as it was for the Italians of the Renaissance or for the British of our own time.
In this sense, the Mediterranean is historical and therefore dialectical. It changes according to the law of dialectical triads.
But by itself, outside its relation to human beings, it does not change in this way at all. It remains eternally what it is.
Taken by itself, therefore, it has nothing to do with dialectic.
More generally, the natural world is dialectical only insofar as it enters into interaction with what is human in human beings and thereby becomes part of the historical world.
But this interaction does not necessarily change the natural side of the world physically, as work does when it builds roads, digs canals, plants forests, clears woodland, and so on.
The natural world becomes historical—and therefore dialectical—as soon as it becomes the subject of human discourse or, more generally, an object of specifically human experience or consciousness.
A “birch tree,” for example, is not itself dialectical. But the “sensory perception of the birch tree” is dialectical, just as the science of the natural world in general is dialectical.
First, it is the human being as such, insofar as a human being differs from an animal.
Second, it is the ideal and real historical world—the technical and political world—created by human beings.
Third, it is the natural world, not taken in itself but taken as a phenomenon: insofar as it “appears” to a human being or to human consciousness through human knowledge.
The natural world in itself, by contrast, has nothing to do with dialectic.

The claim that the dialectical coincides with the human or historical—and conversely, that the human or historical coincides with the dialectical—can be fully demonstrated only by the System of Philosophy as a whole.
Here, then, I will make only two general remarks that may serve as arguments for my claim that only the human world is dialectical, while the natural world is not.
If we are willing to tolerate an anachronism, we can say that the Greeks discovered the non-dialectical character of the natural world.

They understood that nature is, so to speak, an eternal “thesis” to which it is pointless—and indeed impossible—to oppose an antithesis, unless we choose to regard non-being or nothingness as such an antithesis.
Nature remains eternally unchanged, everywhere and always identical with itself.
And this discovery enabled the Greeks to lay the foundations of genuine science of the natural world—the same structure we are still building today.
All natural science rests on the principle that nature is not historical and does not depend on time.
An oxygen atom was the same before human beings appeared as it was in Pushkin’s time and as it is today, and it will remain the same after humanity has disappeared.
It is only for this reason that exact and unchanging knowledge of it is possible.
